title: Every Tugrik Withdrawal in Mongolia Costs More Than You Think
summary: Pay local merchants by QR code across Asia and Latin America. Connect your bank or card, skip ATM fees, and pay like a local in your own currency with Moreta.
body_markdown:
Mongolia is one of the trickier places in Asia to pay for things as a visitor. Ulaanbaatar has quietly gone digital, the countryside has not, and the payment options that internationally issued cards rely on are thinner on the ground than in Bangkok or Seoul. That combination pushes a lot of travelers toward the two most expensive habits in travel money: withdrawing cash repeatedly from ATMs and accepting whatever exchange rate they are shown. Here are the questions travelers actually ask before landing in Ulaanbaatar, answered directly.


### Do Mongolian ATMs charge fees on foreign cards?


Often, yes. Many machines add their own operator fee on top of whatever your home bank charges for international withdrawals, and your bank's exchange rate markup sits on top of both. The problem compounds because withdrawal limits per transaction tend to be modest relative to what a multi-day trip costs, so travelers end up making several withdrawals and paying the fee stack each time. If you have read about how[avoidable ATM fees work in Thailand](https://moretapay.com/blog/avoid-atm-fees-bad-exchange-rates-thailand-promptpay-2026-2026-08-20) , the mechanics in Mongolia are similar, just with fewer workarounds.


### Should I bring US dollars to exchange, or withdraw tugrik on arrival?


If you are bringing cash to convert, do it in the city, not at the airport. Ulaanbaatar has dedicated currency exchange centers, and the ones locals use downtown generally offer better rates than airport counters or hotel desks. Bring clean, newer bills, because worn or marked notes are sometimes refused or rated lower. Exchanging one larger amount at a good city rate almost always beats several small ATM withdrawals with fees attached. That said, exchanging cash still means carrying cash, so only convert what you genuinely expect to spend in tugrik.


### Will I run into dynamic currency conversion in Mongolia?


Anywhere a card terminal or ATM offers to charge you in your home currency instead of tugrik, treat it as a trap. That offer, known as dynamic currency conversion, lets the machine set the exchange rate, and that rate is built to favor the machine's operator, not you. The rule is simple and has no exceptions in Mongolia: if a screen asks whether you want to pay in dollars, euros, or pounds, always choose tugrik and let a fairer conversion happen on your side.


### Can I just use my credit card everywhere in Ulaanbaatar?


No, and this surprises people who arrive expecting a capital city to take plastic. Larger hotels, supermarket chains, and upscale restaurants usually accept international cards. But the places that make a trip memorable, the hole-in-the-wall buuz spots, the stalls at Narantuul market, the coffee counters near Sukhbaatar Square, the driver you arrange through a guesthouse, frequently do not. Locals at those places are not paying with Visa. They are scanning QR codes with their phones, and cash is the fallback, not cards.


### What are the QR codes I keep seeing at counters in UB?


They belong to Mongolia's local QR payment ecosystem, with QPay codes being the ones you will see most often at shops and restaurants in Ulaanbaatar. The catch for visitors is that paying through these codes normally requires a Mongolian bank account, which rules out tourists and most short-term expats. This is where Moreta Pay changes the math: you can scan the same QR code the locals scan, see the amount, the merchant name, and the exchange rate on your screen before confirming, and pay from a wallet funded by your home bank or card. No Mongolian account, no ATM run, no mystery markup, plus 1% cash back on what you spend. We covered the day-to-day rhythm of this in our earlier piece on[how Ulaanbaatar and the steppe handle payments differently](https://moretapay.com/blog/pay-like-a-local-in-mongolia-qpay-cash-2026-2026-08-18) .


### How much cash do I really need for the countryside?


More than you need in the city, and you should get it before you leave Ulaanbaatar. Ger camps, small sums (shops) in aimag towns, roadside guanz canteens, park entry points, and drivers on multi-day Gobi or Khovsgol trips generally expect tugrik cash. ATMs exist in provincial centers but can be empty, offline, or unfriendly to foreign cards, so do not build your trip around finding one in Dalanzadgad. A sensible approach is to estimate your countryside days, add a buffer, make one planned exchange or withdrawal in UB, and ask for smaller denominations. Breaking a large note at a countryside shop can be genuinely difficult.


### Is there a way to skip foreign transaction fees on online bookings too?


Partly, yes. If you are booking through platforms that support QR-based checkout, such as Trip.com, you can complete the payment through Moreta Pay the same way you would at a physical counter, with the rate shown upfront instead of a foreign transaction fee appearing on your card statement later. For a Mongolia trip where domestic flights and UB hotels often get booked through those platforms, that is a quiet but real saving.


### So what does the cheapest setup for Mongolia actually look like?


Split the trip in two. For Ulaanbaatar, lean on QR payments for everything that displays a code, which covers most shops, cafes, and restaurants, and keep a small amount of tugrik for the exceptions. For the countryside, carry cash, sourced once, in the city, at a fair rate, in small bills. Between those two moves you eliminate the repeated ATM fee stack, the airport exchange counter, and the dynamic currency conversion prompt, which together are where most travelers lose money in Mongolia.


### What should I set up before I fly in?


Two things. First, tell your bank you are traveling so a legitimate withdrawal in Ulaanbaatar does not get frozen at the worst moment. Second, get your QR wallet working while you still have easy connectivity: install Moreta Pay, connect your home bank (US banks via Plaid, ACH, SEPA in Europe, UK Faster Payments, Canadian e-Transfer) or a card, and top up in your own currency.
